newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks end higher on Dow rise, poll hopes.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks end higher on Dow rise, poll hopes.

text.p: Tokyo stocks ended the week higher ahead of Japan's general election on Sunday, boosted by a record high on Wall Street overnight and hopes for a stable government capable of executing policies to help the economy.
The key Nikkei 225 index ended the Friday trading session 188.56 points, or 0.88 percent, higher at 21,612.30. Its December futures gained 200 to end at 21,700.
Market sources said activity was fueled by recent media polls showing that the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) may win a clear majority of seats in Japan's election.
"Institutional investors were buying in anticipation of the elections," said Daiichi Securities analyst Akishige Ishikura. "Futures-linked trade also made the market hum with activity."

During the session, the Nikkei hit a high of 21,788.58, having hurtled past two fierce resistance levels -- the end-September closing high of 21,556 and 21,603, a recent intra-day high. Brokers said the next notch was 22,000.
"There are some investors out there who are really optimistic about the polls," one broker said.
It the election goes as forecast, it would mean an end of a period of weak coalition government, with the LDP returning to the position of sole power it held for nearly four decades until 1993.

"Political leadership has been weak for the past couple of years and anything is better than the current state," Daiichi's Ishikura said. "The market thinks economic and administrative reforms, as well as deregulation measures, have a better chance of getting done under LDP supervision."

Brokers said if the LDP did not win a majority, investors were likely to be sorely disappointed and selling would probably emerge. Market participants would retreat to the sidelines to wait for policies to be cobbled together, they said.
Despite the optimism of domestic investors, foreign investors were likely to remain spectators until the Japanese political picture became clearer, brokers said.
"Foreign investors were net sellers today, but not hugely so," said Paul Migliorato, senior salesperson of Jardine Fleming Securities. "They are are mostly waiting for the elections to end."

Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia, told Reuters Financial Television that an LDP victory would be welcomed by financial markets, but stocks may not post further gains as they had risen in advance.
"The market has largely discounted the LDP victory now -- that is not news anymore," he said. "We may see it move in the opposite direction."
